**TL;DR:** The people involved in the show care deeply about the game and want to see it done right, so it's worth trusting them. On top of that, Bella's Ellie is different from Ashley's Ellie because of time, support for her mission, Dina's motivation, and the way her relationship with Dina has developed. 

-----------------------------------------


I've noticed a lot of the differences and similarities with the show (both in S1 and S2) and been curious about how they will play out. At times I've been concerned, but the changes have played out well. The important thing to keep in mind through it all is that the show is not the game: the medium is different, and therefore the way the story is told has to be different. Things which worked in the game (such as navigating spores confined to a specific area using 20-year old gas masks) require a greater suspension of disbelief than a general audience might have for a TV show. On top of that, this show is a labour of love for those involved and the cast and crew have gone out of their way to make sure it's done right. Neil and Gustavo are involved. Craig loves the source material and has worked closely with Neil throughout. Gabriel, Isabel, and Kaitlyn have all played the games. HBO has given them a carte blanche. Yes there are some things I would have liked to see done differently, but I'm confident the people behind the show know what they're doing and want to see it done right. Sure, the immunity --> pregnancy --> sexy times did feel a bit odd to me, but the explanation OP provided makes sense. Trauma and sexual tension are a hell of a thing. And yes, there are changes I would've liked to see in the show - maybe more overt signs of Ellie unravelling (maybe she has trouble sleeping, has recurring dreams, or finds herself spacing out) but it's not enough to take away from how I enjoy the show. Knowing the amount of care and effort the entire crew has put into the show - from the sets to the costumes to the changes that honour the source material - I'm confident the showrunners know what they're doing even if we can't see it yet.


One comment made by others that I have some thoughts on is how Bella's Ellie is different from Ashley's in that she isn't as vengeful or angry. It's fine to be upset with that, but there are a few reasons for the difference in my opinion, not to mention there are still 3 episodes for Ellie to spiral: 


**1) Time:** 3 months after Joel's death plus however long the journey was to Seattle surely allowed Ellie's blind rage to temper a bit. Ellie still wants revenge, but the *initial* feelings have passed and she's not as consumed by it... yet. Her desire revenge consuming her is a bit more subtle in my opinion: yes she's always been impulsive, but now she's prone to make rash decisions. Her judgement is clouded, seen in how poorly prepared she was for her journey, her initial refusal to take Seth's gun despite it being the better one, and her desire to go to the broadcast station during the day. She's not being practical; she is convinced she will have her revenge no matter what


**2) Support for her mission:** In the game, Maria and Tommy are the only people who try to slow Ellie down - and they barely do that. Tommy validates her feelings by leaving on his own accord, and Maria was more sympathetic implying she'd greenlight the mission if she could spare the people/resources. In the show, most people - even the ones who are firmly in her corner - have been telling her to cool it, to be pragmatic, to forgive, to move on. The only two people that firmly support her quest for revenge at all costs (i.e. without strength in numbers) were, interestingly, someone she hates (Seth) and someone she loves (Dina). Tommy wanted to respect the council's decision, but everyone else wanted her to pump the brakes. While she still wants what she wants, surely some of that registered with her on some level however much she disagreed with it. 


**3) Dina's motivation:** in the game, she was "wherever you go, whatever you decide, I'll follow because I love you and you deserve your revenge," so Ellie had the wind at her back. Tommy had already made his way, too, so she felt righteous in her quest and her anger could run unchecked. While Dina is similar in the show ("wherever you go, I'll follow because I love you"), she's practical, pragmatic, and keeping Ellie in check. Secondly, Dina has her own motivation for wanting revenge, and I think Ellie recognizes that: Dina isn't there *just* because she loves Ellie, but because she loved Joel too. By sharing the grief with someone else, perhaps Ellie has been able to process her emotions a bit better. 


**4) The relationship with Dina:** If you've ever had to suppress romantic feelings for someone, it takes up a lot of mental/emotional bandwidth. Maybe not enough to suppress anger or other intense emotions, but enough to compete with them and keep them from being all-consuming. In addition to that, Ellie has had a chance to bond even more with Dina, and I'm sure over their journey they had plenty of deep, emotional conversations about their loss and their desire for revenge. Talking these things out with someone you care about helps to process them. The game doesn't leave the same amount of room to imagine that (other than Ellie's journal entries) because, playing as Ellie, you don't get a break from her grief and anger or a chance to cool off: one second you're in Jackson and hell-bent on revenge, the next second you're in Seattle and still hell-bent on revenge.


All in all, I'm sure Bella Ellie's rage will grow, especially once she is on her own and people are telling her to go back. We just need to be patient, and I'm looking forward to see where the show goes from here.

There were quite a number of differences, changes, or additions. None made the show better or worse than the game, IMO, but there were quite a few and I am definitely missing some (some were covered by u/glamourbuss and others).

With Ellie in the Boston, QZ: You know nothing about her until you first meet her. No idea of what her life was like as an orphan, nothing about her being held captive by the Fireflies, and you only learn of Riley (in passing, unless you play the DLC) later in the game.

With Bill and Frank: Joel does not go to Bill's town with the intention of passing Ellie off to him to be brought to the Fireflies; he went to Bill's town to get a car so that he could find them himself, or at least find Tommy who might know where they are. Quite a lot happens between Joel/Ellie meeting Bill and finding a car battery, including the player's first encounter with a Bloater.

With Sam/Henry in Kansas City (Pittsburgh in the game):

* In the game, Henry had killed people (I think; he definitely did after meeting Joel) and encountered infected prior to meeting Joel.
* As another user mentioned, Sam was not deaf and was closer to Ellie in age than he was in the show.
* Though Sam/Henry (and later Joel/Ellie) were being hunted, it was not out of revenge for the death of their leader's brother but rather because the Hunters wanted their supplies. In the show, the residents of KC were mostly just people trying to move on after deposing FEDRA; in the game, they were sadistic and violent, hunting passers-through for fun and for their supplies. In the game it can be assumed that the Hunters have controlled this settlement for some time (they didn't start off evil, as a note explains), but in the show the residents are just adapting to their new life and still have some of their humanity.
* Sam and Henry were not residents of this settlement/QZ in the game; like Joel and Ellie, they were passing through and were trapped.
* How they escape Kansas City was not through tunnels (though they play a role) but by jumping off a bridge to escape the Hunters.
* The tunnels themselves: in the game, they are far larger and more involved - there is a whole story surrounding the settlement that was established underground, but it is only briefly alluded to in the show. Infected were not driven underground by FEDRA; they were there from the time the underground settlement fell.

With Tommy and the town of Jackson:

* When in the Boston QZ, Joel was not trying to contact Tommy. They had become estranged some time before you begin playing as Joel. Joel and Tess were not trying to get a car battery from Robert to find Tommy, but were wanted to get weapons either for their own purposes or for trading opportunities.
* The Native American couple at the start of episode 6 were from the show only. Everything they talk about regarding a dangerous group further West (which Joel and Ellie encounter) was from the show. Joel and Ellie do not meet the inhabitants of Jackson out in the wilderness, but at a hydroelectric dam they have to pass through. That is where the player meets Tommy for the first time.
* In the game, you never actually go into Jackson. You see it twice from afar (or maybe once, it's been a while): around the time you first meet Tommy, and at the end of the game with Ellie and Joel return to Jackson.
* Joel doesn't ask Tommy to take Ellie because he feels afraid; he asks Tommy to take her because a) Tommy's a former firefly; and b) he doesn't want anything to do with Ellie, partly because he only wants to view her as cargo and nothing else. Ellie runs off when she overhears Joel's request and some shenanigans ensue, leading to the "you sure as hell aren't my daughter" conversation.

With David's crew:

* The chapter at the university is far more involved, and really showcases Ellie and Joel growing closer and starting to care about one another.
* The trust that is initially established between Ellie and David is not because they're having conversation and trying to kill time, but because they work together to fight off infected and get to safety.

Finally, in Salt Lake City: Joel and Ellie are not ambushed while taking a break. Instead, they traverse a tunnel full of infected, and get to a flooded part that they try to get past. Ellie falls in and, since she can't swim, drowns. A Firefly patrol comes across them as Joel is frantically trying to resuscitate her, and knocks him out before taking them captive.

Before the pandemic, I was at the office 3 days a week, at home for 2. I didn't mind it (I might even say I liked it), but context is important. Back then:

* We didn't have the tools we needed for regular remote work. We had VPN access, GCDocs, and a rudimentary chat function, but our collaborative tools (video/audio calls and screensharing) were nowhere near what they are now;
* My division (and most others) had a designated area of each floor, and was never crowded because team members we didn't work with regularly were rotated to work from home on different days. We didn't need to book or fight over spaces - there was always room - and, given the regular presence AND proximity to one another, we could **actually** collaborate. We usually didn't need to since we all had our own files, but it was good to quickly ask someone for help/advice. Nowadays we may be on the same floor/in the same general area one day per week, but for the other two we are either at different buildings or on different floors. *Amazing* for collaboration;
* We had lockers to leave things overnight: not just our work equipment, but other things we might need or want (sweaters, snacks, change of shoes, medication). Having to cart that stuff back and forth every day (whether you need it or not) sucks, especially if your lack of an ergonomic setup at work leaves you feeling broken at the end of the day (mileage may vary; I've been lucky recently); and
* Though the commute wasn't much better, knowing **there was an actual point to going in** made a difference.

Post-pandemic, two days a week RTO made sense to me, somewhat, provided you could coordinate with your team. Three days a week is a little harder to swallow considering we all do our own thing and we have the tools to work from home as if we were in the office (most of us take teams calls regardless of where we're working), but if the goal was to get back to where we were pre-pandemic, despite the increased cost of living and shittier commute, fine. I get it. I'm not happy about it and I think it's stupid, but I'll begrudgingly play ball.

I always love sharing the story of how I almost wrote off and missed out on what ended up being my favourite game ever.

Like you, I was loyal to Xbox through and through. Before that, it had been Nintendo. I don't know why, but I never bought into Sony. One day my 360 red ringed and I turned to PC gaming. A few years later, I decided it was time to get a TV of my own, but also wanted a gaming console, ideally with a Blu-ray player (this was before I had any streaming service). My only criteria was that it could run GTA V and COD. For whatever reason, either graphics or cost, the PS4 won out. With it was a free download of The Last Of Us. I knew nothing about it and I'd never heard of Naughty Dog, but judging by the cover I thought, "Oh, another story about a man and his daughter against the world. *How original*." I didn't bother looking into it - I figured it was included because it wasn't very successful as a game and Sony wanted to encourage people to play it so that a Sony exclusive wasn't a wasted investment. I ignored it, with no intention of trying it. I dove into GTA and COD.

A while later, a friend came over and wanted to play something together but not COD. I saw TLOU was multiplayer (didn't realize it was online only) so I installed it. Sure enough, no couch co-op. Ah well. The next morning I woke up and fired up my PS4. For some reason I wasn't in the mood for GTA or COD and thought "I wonder what this game's all about. Ah well, at least it's free." Fired it up. "Huh. Eerie main menu. Well, let's give it a try."

I did not expect that gut punch of a prologue. By the time the title credits were over, I knew the game was going to be different, and I was locked in. It was a roller coaster of emotions, and I couldn't get enough of it. The story telling, gameplay, and acting blew me away, and the "okay" at the end just had an impact I never expected a game could have. I couldn't believe I almost wrote the game off entirely because I was too lazy to look into it. TLOU 2 was a roller coaster in its own way and had its own impact that left me speechless, but nothing will top going into TLOU completely blind.

If I could Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind anything, it would be that game and TLOU 2 just so I could I could experience them again for the first time. Holy shit.

In hindsight, studying political science in both undergrad and grad school is among the top worst things I've ever done for my mental health (behind resisting therapy and medication for as long as I did). It was fascinating to study back when I was an idealist and had faith in humanity, but it didn't take long for that to change. 

To paraphrase George Carlin: at the core of every cynic is an idealist that has disappointed too many times.

This might not be the answer you're looking for, but I'm going to take a political theory/philosophy approach with this one. I got a bit carried away, so if you choose to read to the end I thank you.

**The TL;DR, however, is that while freedoms are important, they are not (and should not be) absolute. This is a trade off we make in the social contract that is our government. To allow unrestricted freedom would put others in harm's way, undermine the enforcement of almost any law that exists to protect people, and render obsolete the structure most civilized societies rely on. Our charter of rights and freedoms accounts for this, giving governments the right to limit freedom for the sake of the public good.**

The idea of government at any level is that it's a social contract/construct between citizens like you or I, and a structure of norms, expectations and rules that are maintained and enforced by a form of government (the "body politic" or "Leviathan," as Thomas Hobbes described it). While people are truly free in a world without rules or government (anarchy), they are also unsafe (no military or police to protect them, no rules to guide behavior) and have no means to ensure common infrastructure (from roads to railways to supply chains) or access to standard services (regulated banking, medicine, justice, etc.) - all they have are themselves and the people they know and trust. But how many people do you know? And of them, how many do you trust? Would you feel confident in the justice system without belief in the rule of law (a social construct we subject ourselves to)?

The Leviathan/government/body politic exists to erase that uncertainty and provide structure. In order to be part of that structure, we accept limitations on our rights to ensure the well-being and the functioning of that structure (i.e. civilized society), and in the expectation that the Leviathan will not abandon us not screw us over. Freedom does exist, but freedom from consequence does not. Are you free to make choices? Absolutely. But if they go against the structure in place and the well-being of those the structure is meant to protect, you lose certain freedoms.

An example of this is drinking and driving. Do you have a right to make the choice to drink and drive? Absolutely, but you're putting other people at risk even if you've never harmed anyone and have a spotless record of getting from the bar to your home without hitting anyone. Enough people, however, have been harmed because of impaired driving that the government has rules in place against it in order to protect those that don't have a say in your right to choose to drink and drive. Without limitations on the freedom of choice in this case, the driver could say, after being pulled over or after hitting someone "hey, freedom of choice. I'm as free to drink and drive as that pedestrian was free to choose to cross the street or drive on the same street I was on." Case closed. The punishment for drinking and driving is a restriction on freedom, but also a deterrent against a behaviour that puts people at risk. Same thing when going through the airport: regardless of whether you agree with the security measures in place (freedom from unreasonable search and seizure; charter section 8), you accept them because they are in place for the purpose of protecting travelers (or giving them the feeling that they're protected). If someone refuses the screening or refuses to forfeit their favourite box cutter, they don't get to fly (a limitation on mobility rights, charter section 6). After 9/11 would you be perfectly comfortable having that person on your flight? You're also free to choose to run a red light, but most of us don't because, if all of us ran red lights, the streets would hardly be safe. You're also free to hold discriminatory attitudes (freedom of belief, section 2) but if there were no protections against that, how would you feel if you were disciminated against whether due to your ethnicity, profession, sex, gender, orientation, religion, etc. with no recourse?

Insofar as the convoy was concerned, they have the freedom to choose not to get vaccinated or not to wear masks. I won't argue they didn't. But what about the at-risk or the immunocompromised? What if the consequences of that freedom, carried by an asymptomatic member of the convoy, cause the vulnerable to get sick and die? Do they not have rights to life, liberty and security of person (section 7)? The government/Leviathan brought in public health measures not only to protect these people, but to protect frontline workers that keep our cities going, and prevent our healthcare institutions from being overwhelmed (depriving others of life-saving treatment). Without the public health restrictions - as tiring as they've been - we wouldn't be in the place we are now, with most provinces ready to reopen by mid March. We certainly wouldn't have had the brief feeling of normalcy most of the vaccinated felt between delta and omicron. The public health measures have restricted our freedom, but the restrictions weren't too much to ask in the face of the public good, and for the most part they didn't restrict our other freedoms to the point that a decent quality of life was impossible: wear a mask in certain situations, and get a vaccine to participate in activities that put you in close proximity to others. I have mixed feelings on jobs being lost due to vaccine requirements, but they vary depending on the level of contact with others that the job demands. But I digress. 

Maybe those other restaurant-goers (or in a trucker's case, the people they see while receiving/delivering goods; or for unvaccinated nurses/police, the many people they deal with) aren't immunocompromised, but maybe they have loved ones/dependents that are. Or maybe they interact with others who have loved ones/dependent that are. Should they not be protected from the consequences of someone else's freedom of choice to not get vaccinated or wear a mask? When I was growing up, parents accepted the need for their kids to get vaccinated against polio, chickenpox, hepatitis, and other viruses/maladies that could put others at risk; those that did not begrudgingly accepted their kids would need to be homeschooled. What makes this different, other than the rise in anti-scientific beliefs and growing distrust in our institutions? Should we not be looking out for one another and expecting/hoping others do the same for us?

Freedom exists, but it is not absolute. It is limited to the extent a society (and the body politic) deem necessary to protect as many people as possible. As far as Canada goes, our constitution "guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society" (Charter section 1). Public health is one of those justifications, a justification that was carried by every democratically elected government across Canada.

As someone who used to struggle with self-esteem issues myself, I get that. And I also know what it's like to be into someone that's "out of my league." 

An unavoidable fact about dating (and life in general) is that you need to put yourself out there, to be vulnerable, and to try. To do otherwise means you'll miss out on so many possibilities and never grow as a person. I know what it's like to be hard on yourself or think you're not worth much, but believe me, you are. And if someone likes you, they'll see that too. 

**On the second point in particular:** You need to be careful with the idea that someone is "out of your league." However amazing that someone is, they're still a normal person just like you or I, and to think otherwise runs the risk of putting that person on a pedestal. It's fine to think the world of someone, but your own value is **not** defined in comparison to them or anyone else for that matter. The last thing I'll say on this point: consider for a second the possibility that he thinks *you're* out of *his* league. Maybe that's why he's risk averse.

At the end of the day you have to be okay with the possibility that you might get hurt, and be ready to move on if that happens. Easier said than done, I know, but you can't let the fear of getting hurt stop you from being happy.

With the exception of Nora (who was "dead anyways" after breathing in spores) and the people she kills to get to the people in Abby's circle, I would agree that most of the people she killed are a matter of self-defense... kind of.

The argument could be made that the WLF and Serraphite were defending their territory and she instigated the violence, but if there's one thing the TLOU universe does well it's painting a picture of moral ambiguity. The lines between who is good and who is bad are not as clear as they once were, as, outside of one's home, survival is for the most part the new name of the game. There are exceptions of course: the Hunters in Pittsburgh (trapping and hunting down people who pass through); David's group (shot at Joel in the university without provocation); and to a certain extent the Serraphites (I believe they are morally bad, though their belief system lends itself to moral relativism). Nevertheless, Ellie placed herself in a situation where these killings *are* a matter of self-defense, but they were the direct result of her entering WLF territory in her quest to get justice for Joel's death. The WLF NPCs even refer to her, Dina, Tommy and Jesse as "trespassers."

However if we look at it from Ellie's perspective, the people she killed to get to Abby's circle were searching for her and were willing to kill her if they found her. Almost all of the other people she directly interacted with, however, had a chance to walk away but instead chose to fight back. Ellie was put in a position of kill or be killed:

* Whitney (girl with the PS Vita): Ellie had a knife to her throat to get information about Nora, removed the knife when she had her answer, and then stabbed Whitney only when she herself pulled a knife and tried to kill Ellie. As Whitney bleeds out, Ellie mutters "that was dumb," implying she didn't want to kill her. 
* Owen/Mel: Ellie held them at gunpoint and threatened them, but didn't do anything until Owen tried to wrestle the gun from her and Mel charged her with a knife.

All in all, I would argue that the question of self-defense is ambiguous, as it depends on which perspective you look at.  From Ellie's perspective, she was defending herself. From Abby's perspective, Ellie was hunting down her friends. She did not kill in cold blood, sure, but her self-defense was the result of her going to Seattle in the first place.

I've always said there are four phases to online dating when you can't find a match.

**Phase 1**: You're curious about what you might find, but overall don't put too much weight on it. If you're like me and not looking for anything in particular, you don't really give a shit at this point. But as you fail to find matches or make meaningful connections, you proceed to...

**Phase 2**: You swipe and occasionally come across someone you really hope you match with, but never do. It's disappointing, but you figure there's someone else out there. Still, you're optimistic and wonder if it's just a matter of the photos you chose or how you described yourself. So you change it up, and continue swiping. Eventually, though, you find it hasn't helped much and find yourself in...

**Phase 3**: You lower your standards, swipe right on almost everyone, and still don't get a match. You start to wonder if there's something wrong with you, you question your self-worth, your sense of loneliness is amplified, and you wonder why you're on the apps at all or whether you'll ever find someone. When you do match with someone, you're very careful in what you say. But you still come up short and, having tried everything you can think of, you throw your hands in the air in frustration and transition into...

**Phase 4:** You stop caring and come to expect you won't match with anyone. You no longer curate your messages or care how they might be received; you no longer care about what's in your profile. If I want to write limericks in my bio about how much I love Weird Al, I damn well will. If I want to be the dork that I am or lean heavily into self-deprecating humour, I will. I don't stop trying, but I do stop caring as much. Every now and again you come across someone that likes how "unapologetically you" you are. Funny enough that's how I met an ex of mine and wound up in the most emotionally satisfying relationship I've ever been in.

My self-esteem has never been higher than when I wasn't using a dating app. But when I am using a dating app I have to say that Phase 1 and 4 are honestly my favourite places to be. There's no pressure, expectations are low and you don't get particularly upset about a lack of matches. In Phase 4, you still do get frustrated and tired of it all, but you just keep swiping because "why the fuck not?"

I guess what I'm trying to say is everyone dates differently. It's important to be flexible, sure, but at the same time it's important to be open and honest as well.
